title: ROMANS 3:23 TELLS YOU THE BAD NEWS. BUT THE VERY NEXT VERSE REVEALS SOMETHING THAT COULD CHANGE YOUR ETERNITY.
paragraphs: ROMANS 3:23 TELLS YOU THE BAD NEWS. BUT THE VERY NEXT VERSE REVEALS SOMETHING THAT COULD CHANGE YOUR ETERNITY.

You have probably heard that everyone has sinned and fallen short of God's glory. But what if the verse you memorized about your guilt was never meant to be read without the verse that announces God's grace? The difference between Romans 3:23 and Romans 3:24 is only one verse. But what happens between them is the heart of the Gospel.
There is something heartbreaking about a person who believes God can forgive everybody except them.

They sit in church. They sing the worship songs. They know when to say amen. They might even encourage someone else who is struggling, telling them that Jesus loves them and that His mercy never runs out.
But when the lights go off, when the phone becomes silent, when there is nobody left to impress, a different conversation begins inside their heart.
You know what you did.
You know what you keep going back to.
You know the promises you made to God and broke before the week was over.
And somewhere between the shame of yesterday and the fear of tomorrow, they begin to wonder whether the grace they preach to other people could possibly reach someone like them.
Maybe you know that feeling.
Maybe you have asked God for forgiveness so many times that you are embarrassed to ask again.
Maybe there is a chapter of your life you would rather die than have someone read aloud.
Maybe your family sees a responsible person. Your friends see someone who has everything together. Your church sees a faithful believer.
But God sees what nobody else sees.
And that thought terrifies you.
Because what happens when the God who knows everything about you finally confronts everything you have tried to hide?
That is where Romans 3:23 meets us.
Not in the comfortable version of Christianity where everyone looks clean, everyone sounds spiritual, and nobody admits how deeply sin has wounded them.
It meets us in the truth.
And the truth is devastating.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23, KJV
Read those words again.
All have sinned.
Not just the murderer.
Not just the adulterer.
Not just the person who abandoned their family, betrayed a friend, stole money, or destroyed someone's trust.
All.
The preacher who stands behind the pulpit.
The worship leader who sings with tears in their eyes.
The parent trying to raise godly children.
The young believer who sincerely wants to live for Christ.
The person who has never stepped inside a church.
And you.
And me.
Paul leaves no secret doorway through which religious people can escape the verdict.
In the original Greek, Romans 3:23 begins:
πάντες γὰρ ἥμαρτον καὶ ὑστεροῦνται τῆς δόξης τοῦ θεοῦ
Pantes gar hēmarton kai hysterountai tēs doxēs tou theou.
A faithful translation is:
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
The Greek word ἥμαρτον (hēmarton) means “sinned.” It comes from hamartanō, the verb used for sinning or failing to do what is right.
People sometimes explain sin simply as “missing the mark.” That image can be helpful, but Paul's meaning is far more serious than an innocent mistake.
Sin is not merely failing to reach our personal potential.
It is our moral failure before a holy God.
It is rebellion against His rightful authority.
It is loving created things more than the Creator.
It is choosing our own way when we were made to live for His glory.
And then Paul uses another important word:
ὑστεροῦνται (hysterountai) — “fall short” or “lack.”
The form of the verb is present tense, describing humanity's continuing failure to possess or attain the glory of God as we ought.
Notice something painful here.
Paul does not say that we fell short because we did not try hard enough to become successful.
He says we fall short of the glory of God.
Not the expectations of our parents.
Not the standards of our church.
Not the approval of our friends.
God's glory.
His holiness. His righteousness. His perfect goodness.
And suddenly our favorite excuses begin to collapse.
At least I'm not as bad as that person.
But that person is not the standard.
At least I go to church.
Church attendance cannot erase guilt.
At least I help people.
Good works do not make past sins disappear.
At least I believe in God.
Even demons believe that God exists and tremble, according to James 2:19.
The question is not whether we can find somebody whose life looks worse than ours.
The question is whether we are righteous before the God whose holiness exposes every hidden motive.
And Romans 3:23 answers with a verdict that should silence every boasting mouth.
We have sinned.
We have fallen short.
We cannot save ourselves.
But please, do not close your Bible here.
Because Romans 3:23 was never meant to be the end of the sentence.
And if you stop reading at the bad news, you will miss the very reason Paul exposed our guilt in the first place.
The next verse does not begin by telling sinners to become more impressive.
It does not say, “Try harder, and perhaps God will accept you.”
It does not say, “Clean yourself up first, and then you may approach Him.”
Instead, Romans 3:24 announces something so extraordinary that religious pride struggles to comprehend it and wounded hearts struggle to believe it.
“Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 3:24, KJV
Did you see that?
The people who have sinned and fallen short are being confronted with the possibility of justification.
Not through their achievements.
Not through their reputation.
Not through a lifetime of religious performance.
But freely, by His grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.
Here is where the Gospel begins to overturn everything we thought we understood about earning God's acceptance.
The original Greek says:
δικαιούμενοι δωρεὰν τῇ αὐτοῦ χάριτι διὰ τῆς ἀπολυτρώσεως τῆς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ
Dikaioumenoi dōrean tē autou chariti dia tēs apolytrōseōs tēs en Christō Iēsou.
A faithful rendering is:
“Being justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.”
Look carefully at the word δωρεάν (dōrean).
It means freely, gratuitously, or without payment from the recipient.
Not at a discounted price.
Not after earning enough spiritual points.
Not after proving you will never struggle again.
Freely.
And the word χάριτι (chariti) comes from charis, meaning grace or favor.
God's grace is not a paycheck handed to people who have earned His approval.
It is His undeserved favor given to those who cannot establish their own righteousness before Him.
But do not misunderstand this.
Free to us does not mean cheap.
And grace does not mean God simply decided that sin no longer matters.
Paul's next words explain why.
“Through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.”
The Greek word ἀπολύτρωσις (apolytrōsis) refers to redemption, release, or deliverance associated with a ransom.
Paul is announcing that the salvation we could never purchase for ourselves comes through the redeeming work of Jesus Christ.
And this is where the story becomes almost unbearable in its beauty.
Because the God whose glory we have fallen short of did not lower His holiness to make sin acceptable.
He sent His Son to accomplish what sinners could never accomplish.
Jesus entered our broken world.
He was born of a woman.
He experienced hunger, weariness, rejection, sorrow, betrayal, and suffering.
He was tempted, yet without sin, as Hebrews 4:15 teaches.
He loved perfectly where we have loved selfishly.
He obeyed the Father where we have rebelled.
He spoke truth where we have lied.
He remained faithful where we have compromised.
And then the only truly sinless man who ever walked this earth was nailed to a Roman cross.
Not because He had committed some hidden crime.
Not because He deserved condemnation.
But because, in the Father's saving purpose, Christ gave Himself for sinners.
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.” — 2 Corinthians 5:21, KJV
Do not rush past that verse.
The One who knew no sin stood in the place of sinners.
The One who deserved no punishment willingly bore suffering for our salvation.
The One who had never rebelled against the Father gave Himself for those who had.
Isaiah had spoken centuries earlier:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities.” — Isaiah 53:5, KJV
The Hebrew text begins:
וְהוּא מְחֹלָל מִפְּשָׁעֵנוּ מְדֻכָּא מֵעֲוֹנֹתֵינוּ
Vehu mecholal mippesha'enu, medukka me'avonoteinu.
Meaning:
“But he was pierced because of our transgressions, crushed because of our iniquities.”
The Hebrew פְּשָׁעֵנוּ (pesha'enu) means “our transgressions” or “our rebellions.”
And עֲוֹנֹתֵינוּ (avonoteinu) means “our iniquities” or “our guilt.”
Isaiah 53 describes the suffering servant bearing the consequences of the sins of others. Christians understand this prophecy as fulfilled in the suffering and saving work of Jesus Christ.
Our transgressions.
Our iniquities.
Not His.
Ours.
That is why the cross cannot be reduced to a religious decoration, a sentimental story, or an inspirational example of courage.
At Calvary, the holiness of God and the mercy of God were not enemies.
God did not abandon His justice to show mercy.
Romans 3:25–26 explains that God presented Christ in relation to His atoning blood, demonstrating His righteousness so that He would be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus.
This is the Gospel.
Not that sin is harmless.
Not that everybody is automatically saved regardless of faith.
Not that repentance is unnecessary.
But that God has provided in Jesus Christ the righteousness and redemption that guilty sinners desperately need.
And Jesus did not remain in the grave.
On the third day, He rose from the dead.
The resurrection was not an optional happy ending added to an otherwise tragic story.
It was the triumphant declaration that the crucified Savior lives.
Paul writes in Romans 4:25 that Jesus was delivered for our offenses and raised for our justification.
The cross and the empty tomb belong together.
Without the cross, we have no atoning sacrifice.
Without the resurrection, our faith is vain, as 1 Corinthians 15:17 declares.
But Christ has risen.
And because He lives, the Gospel is not merely a memory of something beautiful that happened long ago.
It is God's living announcement of salvation through His Son.
Now think about the person you were before you began hiding your wounds behind a smile.
Think about the things you regret.
The words you wish you could take back.
The relationships you damaged.
The temptations you entertained.
The secret compromises.
The moments when you knew what was right and deliberately chose what was wrong.
Perhaps you are carrying the consequences of something that happened years ago.
Perhaps you hurt someone who has never forgiven you.
Perhaps someone hurt you, and in trying to survive the pain, you began making choices that wounded you even more.
Perhaps you have been living with a terrible assumption:
God may tolerate me, but He could never delight in saving someone like me.
Listen carefully.
Romans 3:23 tells the truth about your sin.
Romans 3:24 tells the truth about the grace God has provided in Jesus Christ.
You need both truths.
If you deny the first, you will never understand why you need a Savior.
If you ignore the second, you may mistake conviction for hopeless condemnation.
And the Gospel calls you away from both self-righteousness and despair.
You are more sinful than your carefully managed image admits.
But Christ is a greater Savior than your shame has allowed you to believe.
That does not mean every consequence of your past disappears overnight.
It does not mean wounded relationships instantly heal.
It does not mean people you harmed are obligated to trust you again without evidence of repentance and change.
And it certainly does not mean you can continue deliberately in sin because grace is available.
Paul anticipates that very distortion in Romans 6:1–2:
“Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid.”
Grace is not God's permission slip for rebellion.
Grace is God's saving favor that brings us into a new relationship with Him and teaches us to turn away from ungodliness.
Titus 2:11–12 makes that connection unmistakable.
The grace that brings salvation also teaches us to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts.
So when Jesus calls sinners to Himself, He does not say that their sin is beautiful.
He offers something infinitely better.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
New life.
Transformation.
A future that no longer has to be ruled by the guilt of the past.
And this is where I want you to think about a woman whose life was marked by public shame.
In John 8:1–11, a woman accused of adultery was brought before Jesus.
The religious leaders were not approaching Him with tender concern for her restoration.
They were using her situation to test Him.
Imagine the humiliation.
The staring faces.
The accusation.
The fear.
The awareness that everyone in that crowd knew what she had been accused of doing.
She was no longer being treated as a person with a name, a history, and a soul.
She had become a scandal.
A public example.
A weapon in someone else's religious argument.
But Jesus refused to participate in their hypocrisy.
When they continued pressing Him, He answered:
“He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her.” — John 8:7, KJV
One by one, her accusers left.
And when Jesus asked whether anyone had condemned her, she answered that no one had.
Then came His remarkable words:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” — John 8:11, KJV
Notice what Jesus did not do.
He did not declare adultery righteous.
He did not tell her that repentance was unnecessary.
He did not pretend holiness was irrelevant.
But neither did He join the crowd in crushing her beneath public humiliation.
He showed mercy while calling her away from sin.
The passage illustrates a beautiful truth consistent with the Gospel: Christ's mercy does not require Him to approve of what destroys us.
His mercy calls us into a different life.

There is a textual detail worth knowing: John 7:53–8:11 is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts of John's Gospel, and many modern Bibles mark the passage accordingly. We should be transparent about that rather than hide it. The central biblical truths of Jesus' mercy toward sinners and His call to repentance are firmly established elsewhere in Scripture, including Luke 7:36–50, Luke 19:1–10, and John 5:14.
And perhaps that is what somebody reading this desperately needs to understand.
Jesus does not have to call your sin acceptable in order to offer you forgiveness.
He does not need to rewrite the moral truth about your past.
He offers to rewrite the future of a repentant sinner through His redeeming grace.
Not because the scandal was imaginary.
Not because the damage was insignificant.
Not because the consequences were always avoidable.
But because Jesus Christ can redeem people who could never redeem themselves.
Consider Peter.
He promised loyalty.
He insisted he would never abandon Jesus.
And then, when fear surrounded him, he denied knowing the Lord three times.
Luke 22:61 records that Jesus turned and looked at Peter.
Can you imagine that moment?
The sound of the rooster.
The memory of the promise.
The realization of what he had just done.
And the eyes of the Savior he had denied.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
There are tears that come from getting caught.
And there are tears that come from finally seeing what sin has done.
Peter knew the pain of failure.
But his story did not end beside that courtyard fire.
After His resurrection, Jesus restored Peter in John 21, confronting him with the question of love and commissioning him to care for His sheep.
Peter's denial was real.
His sorrow was real.
His restoration was real.
And the grace of Christ was greater than the failure that had threatened to define him.
Now remember the thief on the cross.
He had no opportunity to rebuild a respectable public reputation.
No years left to prove his transformation through an impressive religious résumé.
No lifetime of good works to present as payment for salvation.
But he turned to Jesus and said:
“Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.” — Luke 23:42, KJV
And Jesus answered:
“Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” — Luke 23:43, KJV
That dying man did not purchase paradise.
He had no righteousness of his own with which to negotiate his acceptance.
He looked to the crucified King.
And Jesus gave him a promise.
This is not a reason to postpone repentance until the last possible moment.
It is a reason never to imagine that your remaining strength, your achievements, or your religious reputation are what make Christ able to save you.
The Savior is sufficient.
His grace is not weak.
His blood is not powerless.
His resurrection is not an empty symbol.
And His invitation is not restricted to people whose past is easy to explain.
But there is something important we must not leave unsaid.
Romans 3:24 cannot be separated from Romans 3:22 and Romans 3:25–26.
Paul speaks of the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe.
He speaks of Christ's atoning work and of God justifying the one who has faith in Jesus.
The Gospel does not announce that every human being is automatically justified merely because everyone has sinned.
It announces that justification is God's gracious gift through Christ, received by faith.
That distinction matters eternally.
Because salvation is not earned by good works, but neither is saving faith simply admiring Jesus from a distance while refusing His lordship.
Jesus calls us to repent and believe the Gospel (Mark 1:15).
Repentance is not paying God back for your sins.
It is turning from sin toward God.
Faith is not a religious achievement that makes you worthy of grace.
It is trusting Jesus Christ as the Savior you cannot replace and the Lord you cannot rightfully ignore.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
And verse 10 continues by explaining that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Do you see the order?
We are not saved because our good works have made us righteous.
We are saved by grace through faith, and God's transforming work produces a new way of living.
Good works are the fruit of salvation, not its purchase price.
This matters because some of you have spent years trying to pay a debt that Jesus alone could satisfy.
You serve until you are exhausted.
You give until you feel empty.
You say yes to every request because somewhere inside you are afraid that God will stop loving you if you ever say no.
You think spiritual exhaustion is proof of faithfulness.
You confuse being needed by people with being accepted by God.
And perhaps you have even begun treating every act of generosity as a payment toward forgiveness.
But listen.
You cannot buy what Christ has already accomplished.
Not with money.
Not with ministry.
Not with tears.
Not with promises.
Not with the number of Bible verses you memorize.
Not even with the number of people you lead to church.
Your salvation rests on Jesus Christ, not your ability to make yourself indispensable.
And this truth should change the way we think about Christian giving, too.
Because when grace truly captures a heart, generosity can begin to flow from gratitude rather than fear.
The early believers supported the work of the Gospel.
They shared resources.
They cared for those in need.
They helped sustain ministry.
Paul taught that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support from those who benefit from their ministry (1 Corinthians 9:14; Galatians 6:6).
He also made something equally important clear.
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
Christian generosity is not supposed to be extracted through guilt, threats, or spiritual intimidation.
You can glorify God through obedience, prayer, worship, service, compassion, generosity, and faithful living in countless ways.
But if the Gospel has strengthened you through this ministry, you may also choose to glorify Him by helping that ministry continue.
That is the heart behind Gospel Warrior.
Every article shared.
Every biblical truth explained.
Every struggling believer encouraged to open Scripture again.
Every wounded person reminded that Jesus Christ still calls sinners to repentance, forgiveness, and new life.
It is all part of a mission that matters deeply to us.
And if you have been encouraged, challenged, or strengthened through Gospel Warrior, I want to invite you into something more personal than simply reading another post and moving on.
Not because God will love you more.
And perhaps there is something beautiful about that.
A person who once needed someone to remind them of God's grace can help make that same message available to someone else.
Someone whose faith was strengthened by a single article can help another struggling believer encounter the Word of God.
Someone who found encouragement during a season of spiritual exhaustion can help extend that encouragement to another person who feels forgotten.
Not everyone can preach from a pulpit.
Not everyone can write a book.
Not everyone can devote hours to producing biblical discipleship materials.
But believers can participate in Gospel ministry in different ways, including prayer, encouragement, sharing resources, and voluntary financial support.
These are expressions of appreciation, not spiritual rewards or a way to purchase God's favor.
The greatest treasure we want you to discover is not something you can wear, display, or place on a bookshelf.
It is the surpassing worth of knowing Jesus Christ.
Your worth before God is not measured by what you can contribute financially.
You can still pray.
You can still grow.
You can still share the truth.
You can still help someone encounter the Gospel.
Think about the people who may see it.
A former classmate who has stopped attending church.
A relative who has been silently grieving.
A friend whose marriage is falling apart.
A young person who thinks their past has already disqualified them from God's mercy.
A believer who looks spiritually strong but is secretly losing hope.
Someone who does not yet know Jesus.
You may not know what they are carrying.
You may never hear the full story of what God does in their heart.
But sharing Scripture-centered encouragement gives another person an opportunity to hear the truth.
And sometimes, an ordinary act of sharing becomes the beginning of an extraordinary conversation.
And I want to ask you something that may be more important than anything else you do after reading this.
Which verse have you been living in?
Romans 3:23?
Or Romans 3:24?
Have you been living as though your sin is the final word about you?
Have you spent years remembering everything you did wrong while forgetting what Christ has done for sinners?
Have you been treating your shame as though it possesses greater authority than the Word of God?
Or have you gone in the opposite direction, using the language of grace to excuse a sin you know Christ is calling you to leave behind?
Be honest.
Not for the sake of appearances.
Not because strangers on the internet need access to your private wounds.
But because spiritual honesty matters.
Or share a brief testimony of how Jesus has been teaching you to understand His forgiveness more deeply.
You do not have to reveal confidential details or confess private sins publicly to prove that your repentance is sincere.
But perhaps your words of hope will encourage another person who thought they were the only one struggling.
And perhaps someone will read the comments and discover that the Christian life is not a gathering of people who have never failed.
It is a community of sinners who continually need the grace of God, called to trust and follow the risen Savior.
Now, before you leave, there is one more thing I want you to see.
Something that may change how you read Romans 3 for the rest of your life.
When Paul wrote this passage, he did not place a chapter-ending wall between verse 23 and verse 24.
The original Greek text was not written with the modern verse numbers we use today.
Those divisions were added many centuries later to help readers locate passages.
That means the words we often quote separately are actually part of one connected argument.
Humanity has sinned.
Humanity falls short of God's glory.
And God reveals the gracious justification available through the redemption accomplished in Christ Jesus.
Paul did not expose the wound merely to leave sinners staring at it.
He proclaimed the Savior.
The diagnosis is serious because the disease is deadly.
But the Gospel announces the One who can save.
And suddenly the two verses belong together in a way that should make every self-righteous person humble and every despairing sinner willing to come to Christ.
Romans 3:23 destroys the illusion that we can save ourselves.
Romans 3:24 announces the grace of the God who saves through Jesus Christ.
One verse silences our boasting.
The next directs our attention to redemption.
One reveals our need.
The next reveals God's provision.
One tells us why we cannot stand before God on the basis of our own righteousness.
The next tells us where justification is found.
In Christ Jesus.
Not in the perfection of your repentance.
Not in the strength of your emotions.
Not in the absence of every future struggle.
Not in your ability to erase the consequences of yesterday.
In Christ Jesus.
And if you are reading this with tears in your eyes because you know how badly you have fallen, hear the invitation of the Savior.
Do not run from Him.
Do not wait until you feel worthy.
Do not mistake temporary religious excitement for the new birth.
Come to Christ in repentance and faith.
Confess your sin honestly before God.
Trust the crucified and risen Savior.
Turn from the darkness you have been defending.
Follow Him in the light.
And when you stumble, do not make peace with sin, but do not imagine that hiding from Christ will heal you.
Return to His Word.
Seek His help.
Walk with faithful believers who can encourage you, correct you, pray with you, and help you grow.
Remember 1 John 1:9:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
The Christian life is not built on pretending that sin no longer exists.
It is built on belonging to the Savior who died for sinners and rose again.
And for those who are in Christ Jesus, Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
That is not a promise that sin is harmless.
It is a promise rooted in the saving work of Jesus.
The One who exposes our guilt is also the One who has provided the only sufficient answer to it.
So if you have spent years believing that your worst moment has already determined your eternal destiny, open your Bible again.
Read Romans 3:23.
Let it humble you.
Let it expose every false refuge.
Let it remind you why you need a Savior.
Then keep reading.
Read Romans 3:24.
And do not stop until you have considered the cross, the empty tomb, and the righteousness of God revealed through faith in Jesus Christ.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that you were secretly good enough all along.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ is sufficient to save sinners who could never make themselves good enough.
Your past may explain some of your scars.
Your choices may have consequences that require courage, restitution, patience, and humility.
Your repentance may involve difficult conversations and painful changes.
But none of those realities makes Christ less powerful to save.
The scandal of sin is real.
The holiness of God is real.
The cross is real.
The resurrection is real.
And the grace of God in Jesus Christ is not a fragile hope held together by your ability to perform.
It rests on the finished work of the Savior.
So here is the question I want to leave with you.
When your conscience reminds you of what you have done, will you answer by pointing to what you have accomplished?
Or will you turn in repentance and faith to what Jesus Christ has accomplished?
Because there is no greater freedom than discovering that you do not have to pretend to be innocent in order to come to the Savior of the guilty.
There is no greater hope than knowing that the blood of Jesus Christ is sufficient for the forgiveness of sins.
And there is no greater transformation than the one God begins in those who belong to His Son.
Romans 3:23 tells you why you need saving. Romans 3:24 tells you where salvation is found.
Don't let shame make you stop reading one verse before grace.
